newsitem.title: USA: Century Aluminum regroups, mulls expansion.
newsitem.headline: Century Aluminum regroups, mulls expansion.

text.p: Century Aluminum Co is going back to basics in a bid to carve out a bigger and more profitable role in the increasingly choppy waters of the aluminum industry, with product rationalisation and acquisitions top of the agenda, the company's Chairman and CEO Craig Davis said.
"We have to broaden our business base and reduce our dependency on the rolling business," Davis told Century's first annual stockholder meeting.
"Our focus will be on acquisitions, opportunities in primary aluminum and looking at certain, selected semi-fabricated business," Davis added.
First quarter net income per share was 9 cents, down from 40 cents in the same period last year, with net sales of $191.5 million, up from $181.40 million.
Century, in which Swiss-based privately-held trading powerhouse Glencore International owns 39.9 percent, has been publicly traded on NASDAQ since March last year.
Century owns 26.6 percent of Mt Holly 200,000 tonnes per year smelter in South Carolina. Alumax is the operator with a controlling 50.33 percent.

Century also wholly-owns the Ravenswood 180,000 tonnes per year primary smelter in West Virginia, equipped with a rolling and fabrication plant producing 500 to 600 million pounds a year of 2,500 products.
Both smelters operate at full capacity.
Century sells some of its primary aluminum but has to buy scrap.
Ravenswood was dogged by a long-running labor dispute and poor margins since the turnaround began in the early 1990s, but results so far were still not fully satisfactory, Davis said.

"We are considering restructuring the rolling business to improve profitability," Davis said. "The mill makes too many products whose margins were often too slim. We question whether this is the best way to run the Ravenswood rolling mill. No product or process is sacred."
Century completes its review soon, amid overcapacity in the rolling sector, especially in building sheet and, to a lesser extent, cansheet.
But the company is already doubling its profitable plate capacity to over 50 million pounds a year.
Capital expenditure will be some $40 million annually over the next few years. But money for acquisitions would have to come from a mixture of project financing, and equity.
Key targets would be partnerships with existing primary producers, while brownfield and possibly greenfield expansions were further down the road, Davis said.
Century was also attracted to the extrusions business.
"We would look to keep the debt down to low numbers, about 20 to 30 percent of equity," Davis said. Current debt was $45 million compared with equity of $170 million.
As a small to medium sized producer, Davis is aware of the need to carve out a role in an industry where even the big players such as Reynolds Metals and Kaiser Aluminum are in the throes of change.

"Alcoa seems to have a definite plan and view of where they are going, but a great deal of the rest of the industry is somewhat uncertain about their future," Davis told reporters after the annual meeting. "Worldwide, a lot of companies are questioning why they are in the industry and where they are going to go."

Meanwhile, aluminum prices were expected to remain firm for the rest of this year. "We could see some further improvement, especially if inventory continues to come down," Davis said. "Prices could see a spike in the latter part of the year."

Earnings in the second quarter and further forward were expected to remain similar to the first quarter, but with some improvement in margins for rolled products because recent price hikes have gone through, Davis said. Primary aluminum prices have also picked up.
